A clarinettist and a pianist both read a C, and they play different notes. That is not a mistake.
The clarinet is a **transposing instrument**: its part is written at a different pitch from the one
that sounds. This lesson explains how to work out what sounds, and how scores show it.

## 1. What "in B♭" means

The key in an instrument's name is **the note that sounds when the player reads a written C**.

- **Clarinet in B♭**: written C sounds B♭, a major 2nd lower. Every note sounds a major 2nd lower.
- **Horn in F**: written C sounds F, a perfect 5th lower.
- **Alto saxophone in E♭**: written C sounds the E♭ a major 6th lower.
- **Clarinet in E♭**: written C sounds the E♭ a minor 3rd *higher*. The name gives the note, not the
  direction: small instruments usually sound up, large ones down.

An instrument "in C" (flute, oboe, violin, piano, trombone, voice) is **non-transposing**: it sounds
what it reads.

Here is concert middle C, the same sound, as it is written for five instruments:

## 2. The common transpositions

| Instrument | Written C sounds | Interval |
|---|---|---|
| Piccolo, xylophone, celesta | C | an octave higher |
| Glockenspiel | C | two octaves higher |
| Clarinet in E♭, trumpet in E♭ | E♭ | minor 3rd higher |
| Trumpet in D, clarinet in D | D | major 2nd higher |
| Clarinet, trumpet, cornet, flugelhorn, soprano sax in B♭ | B♭ | major 2nd lower |
| Clarinet in A | A | minor 3rd lower |
| Alto flute in G | G | perfect 4th lower |
| Horn in F, cor anglais | F | perfect 5th lower |
| Alto sax, tenor horn (alto horn) in E♭ | E♭ | major 6th lower |
| Guitar, bass guitar, double bass, contrabassoon, tenor voice | C | an octave lower |
| Tenor sax, bass clarinet, euphonium and brass-band trombone (treble clef) in B♭ | B♭ | major 9th lower (an octave + a 2nd) |
| Baritone sax, E♭ bass (brass band) | E♭ | an octave + a major 6th lower |
| BB♭ bass (brass band) | B♭ | two octaves + a major 2nd lower |

The [Part Reader](/tools/part-reader.qmd) has the full list, including every horn and trumpet key.

## 3. Moving the key signature

The part's key moves **the opposite way** from the sound. If the instrument sounds a major 2nd lower,
its part is written a major 2nd higher.

- Concert **C major** → B♭ clarinet part in **D major** (2 sharps).
- Concert **F major** → horn in F part in **C major**.
- Concert **E♭ major** → alto sax part in **C major**.

A quick rule for keys: a B♭ instrument's part has **two more sharps (or two fewer flats)** than the
concert key; an E♭ instrument's has **three more sharps**; an F instrument's has **one more sharp**; an A
instrument's has **three more flats**.

<div class="sq" data-quiz="keysig"></div>

<div class="sq" data-quiz="reverse"></div>

## 4. Notes, one at a time

To find the sounding note, move the written note by the instrument's interval. Keep the octave
in mind, but for naming notes the letter and accidental are what count.

<div class="sq" data-quiz="sound"></div>

## 5. Octave transpositions and octave discrepancies

Some instruments transpose only by octaves. Their parts keep the concert key signature; only the
register is moved, so the notes sit on the staff instead of on a ladder of ledger lines.

- **Sound higher:** piccolo (8va), xylophone and celesta (8va), glockenspiel (two octaves).
- **Sound lower:** double bass, guitar, bass guitar, contrabassoon, tenor voice (8vb).

**Octave discrepancies to watch:**

- **Same key, different octave.** Soprano sax and tenor sax are both "in B♭", and the B♭ clarinet and
  bass clarinet too. The bigger one sounds an **octave lower** than its smaller sibling. The name says
  the key, not the octave.
- **Doublings that are not unisons.** A cello and double bass reading the same written line play in
  octaves, not in unison. A flute and piccolo on the same written line do too.
- **Guitar and tenor.** A guitar's written middle C sounds the C below. A score that shows the guitar
  at sounding pitch in plain treble clef would have its notes an octave lower than the player reads, deep in ledger lines.
- **Bass clarinet and horn bass clef**: the old conventions in
  [lesson 2](score-multi-clef.qmd#the-octave-traps).

## 6. Transposed scores and concert-pitch scores

A conductor's score comes in one of two forms.

**Transposed score.** Every staff is written as the player reads it. The clarinet staff has a different
key signature from the violins; the horn's notes look a fifth higher than they sound. This is the
traditional form, and it lets the conductor see exactly what each player sees, which helps in rehearsal
("clarinets, your written F♯ in bar 12").

**Concert-pitch score (C score).** Every staff is at sounding pitch, all with the same key signature.
Harmony is far easier to see. Some composers have written whole orchestral scores this way, Prokofiev
among them. Most film, jazz-band and study scores, and the "concert pitch" view in notation software,
work like this too.

**What a concert score still transposes.** Even a C score usually keeps the octave transpositions:
piccolo, glockenspiel, xylophone, celesta, double bass, guitar and contrabassoon are still written in
their own octave, because writing them at sounding pitch would bury them in ledger lines. Always check
the score's preface; it usually says "Score in C" and lists the exceptions.

**How to tell which one you have.** Look at the key signatures at the start. If the clarinets, horns
and trumpets have a different key from the strings, it is transposed. If every staff matches, it is in C
(or the music has no key signature, in which case look for a note at the top of the first page).

<div class="sr-tip">

**Writing parts from a concert score.** Notation software will do it, but check every part: look for
awkward keys (a concert B major gives a B♭ clarinet C♯ major, seven sharps, and you may prefer D♭ major
with five flats), and look for notes outside the instrument's written range.

</div>
